title: THE DIVIDING HATRED: THE GRAFTED IN STRANGERS

sense.text: The Lord stands above Jacob and says, “I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac: the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed”. This is spoken to Jacob, and the land and the promise go to his children.

“And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south”. Jacob’s children are spread abroad to the west, the east, the north and the south of the earth. Israel would be an omnipresent people: whether through captivity, through willful migration or through forced migration, Israel would be scattered everywhere, all over the earth.

“And in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed.” The families of the earth are the Israelite families that would be in those areas, north, south, east and west. The other nations are not getting blessed. Slavery, perpetual employment: that is going to be their blessing.

precepts.why:
God changes his name: “thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name: and he called his name Israel.”

Then: “I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee”. The nation is the southern kingdom, and the company of nations is the northern kingdom. That is why it is written that way. In context you could say it is all twelve tribes, but in prophetic understanding it speaks of the division of the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom, the very division this class is about.

“And kings shall come out of thy loins”: Saul, David, Hezekiah, Josiah. Those are the kings.

sense.text: “He is the Rock, his work is perfect”. That is all about Christ. Don’t let anyone confuse you and say it is somebody else. Christ is the Rock.

“When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel.” Everyone got their land, all separated, but God’s chosen people got the most important land: the promised land.

“For the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.” He found him in the wilderness, led him, instructed him, and “kept him as the apple of his eye.” We are the apple of the Lord’s eye. You touch us, you touch him.

“But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked”. Israel waxed fat: we waxed rebellious, we waxed rich, and we waxed comfortable. Then “he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.” The Rock of our salvation is Christ again.
“They provoked him to jealousy with strange gods, with abominations provoked they him to anger.” Israel provoked the Rock of our salvation to jealousy.
“Of the Rock that begat thee thou art unmindful, and hast forgotten God that formed thee.” The Rock that begat us, that made us, is Christ. That Rock is the God that formed us.

“And when the Lord saw it, he abhorred them, because of the provoking of his sons, and of his daughters.” He got pissed off and started to hate us. The key point is that we provoked our God to anger with the other nations, their idols and the nations themselves.

“I will hide my face from them, I will see what their end shall be: for they are a very froward generation, children in whom is no faith.” Rebellious.

“They have moved me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have provoked me to anger with their vanities”: with idols. “And I will move them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.”

Keep in mind “not a people” and “a foolish nation”. Some will say that is the other nations. No, it is not. He provoked them to anger by dealing with those people in the first place. The rest of the class proves who “not a people” is.
“I write no new commandment unto you, but an old commandment which ye had from the beginning”: from Moses’ time.

“Again, a new commandment I write unto you”. Why is it new? Because Israel was not following it. Going back to the law of Moses, we were children in whom is no faith, rebellious; we waxed fat and kicked.

“He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now.”

Here is an example of that hatred. Imagine your people are in captivity right now, and the people that enslaved them are ruling today. They conspired for hundreds of years and spent billions, maybe trillions, to make sure our history was hidden from us. They tortured us, beat us, raped us, castrated us, and broke us physically, mentally, psychologically and spiritually. When we fell, they came into their heaven: them ruling is their heaven. So what are we in right now? Now imagine me, in the heathen’s hell, teaching the devil in his kingdom the access he has to our heaven. That is hate. You hate your people and you hate yourself, and for that you are in darkness.

Edom is who he was born to be. But the Jacob that tries to save our enemies is despised more than anything else, not with a personal hate but a biblical hatred, because it is an evil spirit and a weakening. Esau does not forget; he holds grudges. Rumor has it that when they took Maduro out, they bombed the mausoleum where Hugo Chavez is buried, because Chavez spoke ill of America and Bush. They don’t forget nothing. But Jacob, in the midst of captivity, forgets.

“He that loveth his brother abideth in the light, and there is none occasion of stumbling in him.” When you despise your brother and your people, you are going to stumble, and stumble in a lot of deep bases.

“But he that hateth his brother is in darkness, and walketh in darkness, and knoweth not whither he goeth, because that darkness hath blinded his eyes.” Darkness, the hate of your brother, will blind your eyes. Keep that in mind: it is very important for the rest of the class.

precepts.why:
“If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” And “he who loveth God love his brother also.”

You can’t love one and hate the other; it is impossible. If you love your brother, by default you love God. If you love God, by default you love your brother. They go hand in hand: God and people, God and race. What the white man promotes among his people is what we should promote among ourselves. When we say it, we’re racist; when they say it, they’re patriots.

Christ said it first: “A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.” Christ said it to the disciples, and John repeated it in his epistle.
“These things I command you, that ye love one another.” Christ said that over and over and over again.

A scribe asks, “Which is the first commandment of all?” Christ answers, “Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength”. “And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. There is none other commandment greater than these.”

None greater, because if you love your brother as yourself you can keep all the commandments; they all go hand in hand. You cannot love God and hate your brother. What Christ is really saying is: love your ways, love your people. The law was given to us because we had learned how to hate one another, and we give the same laws to our people today.

Imagine being so brainwashed in this captivity that you care about your oppressor and forget your own kind while your people are being oppressed. That is a mind destroyed. You’re a dummy, and that is the kindest word for it.

This is where Christ got it from. It was not really new; we heard it before. “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him. Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.”

Your neighbour is your people, your brother. When you despise yourself, you despise your God that resembles you and your brother that resembles you. It is a domino effect. You can’t love one and hate the other.

This is the dividing hatred: Ephraim and Judah began to despise each other, and that is why both fell. The northern kingdom fell first and the southern kingdom afterwards, for the same hatred Moses warned against in the very beginning, when we were all together.

sense.text: “Abram passed through the land unto the place of Sichem, unto the plain of Moreh”, and the Lord said, “Unto thy seed will I give this land: and there builded he an altar unto the Lord”. Sichem, Shechem, is in the hill country of Ephraim. That area is the northern kingdom’s land.

He removed “unto a mountain on the east of Beth–el, and pitched his tent, having Beth–el on the west, and Hai on the east: and there he builded an altar unto the Lord”. Bethel, Ai, Shiloh and Shechem are all in that same area, Ephraim’s land: the northern kingdom’s land. That is where Abraham built the altar, and not far from there Israel received the commandments, the cursings and the blessings.

“Call her name Lo–ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away. But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah”. The northern kingdom would receive no mercy; Judah would be saved by the Lord their God.

“Call his name Lo–ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.” Ephraim is no longer deemed God’s people. When you are not God’s people, what do you become? Gentiles, non-Israelites. Strangers, heathens, uncircumcision, Gentiles: all the same.

“Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea”, like he promised Jacob. “In the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people”, where they were called Gentiles, “there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.”

“Then shall the children of Judah”, that is the nation, “and the children of Israel”, the company of nations, “be gathered together”. Gathered together means they become one. “And appoint themselves one head”: that head is Christ. “For great shall be the day of Jezreel”: Jezreel means the seed of Israel.

precepts.why:
You read the same thing from multiple prophets. “I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all”: one king, one head, Christ. “And they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”: no more southern and northern.

“Neither shall they defile themselves any more with their idols, nor with their detestable things”. They will be gathered together and brought back together, just as Hosea said. And remember: of the two, one is not a nation at all.

The northern kingdom aligned itself with Syria to attack the southern kingdom, its own brother, and this is the prophecy against them for it. “For the head of Syria is Damascus”, the capital of Syria, “and the head of Damascus is Rezin”, the king of the Syrians at that time. “And within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.”

“That it be not a people.” We read that earlier in Deuteronomy 32. So who was Moses talking about when he said he would provoke Israel to jealousy with them which are not a people, with a foolish nation? Ephraim.

sense.text: “Then cometh he to a city of Samaria, which is called Sychar, near to the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.” On the map, Sychar is right there in Samaria. Jacob gave that parcel of land, where Christ met the woman at the well, to Joseph and his children Ephraim and Manasseh.
“Now Jacob’s well was there.” Christ met this woman there, and she is northern kingdom.

“To the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia”. They are called strangers here: the grafted in strangers, not a people, not my people, Lo-ammi, I am not your God. It is all the same, and it refers to the northern kingdom.
“Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father”. Peter calls the strangers scattered in verse 1 the elect. Who is that? Israelites.

precepts.why: Who are the elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father? “For Jacob my servant’s sake, and Israel mine elect”. Israel is the elect, the chosen: the same thing. That is who the elect are that Peter is writing to.

sense.text: The thought does not change: this is still the letter to the strangers. “Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner”. The builders are the southern kingdom: the Pharisees, the Sadducees, the scribes, the elders, the rulers.

“And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence”. Christ becomes a stone of stumbling, the same Rock that begat us in Deuteronomy. “Even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient”: the builders, the elders of the southern kingdom. “Whereunto also they were appointed”: they were reserved to be disobedient so Christ could be killed and die for both kingdoms, to reunite all twelve tribes. That cannot be done unless Christ died.

The builders were appointed to reject Christ, because by rejecting him they would have him killed, and by his being killed he would grant the northern kingdom a chance to repent and be redeemed back into the fold.

“But ye are a chosen generation”. The ye is the strangers of 1 Peter 1:1, the elect of verse 2. Context matters. Chosen goes back to elect. “A royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people”: all Israel is a peculiar people. They should “shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light”.

“Which in time past were not a people”. Sound familiar? These strangers were not a people: that was the promise against the northern kingdom in Isaiah 7:8 and Hosea 1. “But are now the people of God”: when Christ dies he redeems them back into being his people and gathers them together in one. “Which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.” Peter covers both peoples, but the strangers here are primarily the northern kingdom. How could you find that out if you don’t know your history? You would never find it out.

precepts.why:
This is chapter 2 of the same context as Hosea 1:10-11, where he gathers them together again under one head. “And they shall hear Jezreel”: the seed of Israel. “And I will sow her unto me in the earth”: he adopts her back to him in the earth. “And I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people; and they shall say, Thou art my God.”

Peter is quoting Hosea here, the same precept, word for word: not a people, now the people of God; not obtained mercy, now obtained mercy.

Christ out of his own mouth: “I lay down my life for the sheep. And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold”. Christ is of Judah, so this fold is Judah, the southern kingdom. The other sheep are the northern kingdom.

“Them also I must bring”: bring together, like Hosea said and Ezekiel said. “And they shall hear my voice”: both kingdoms shall hear his voice, through Judah, through the teachings of Judah first. “And there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.” Hosea said one head, Ezekiel said one king; Christ says one shepherd, and that shepherd is himself. He is quoting Hosea 1:10-11 and Ezekiel 37:22.

The high priest, as stupid and evil as he was, was moved by the Lord to see it too. Caiaphas said, “it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.” The whole nation is all of Israel: Christ died for all twelve tribes, not for one kingdom only.

“And this spake he not of himself: but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation; And not for that nation only”: that is the northern kingdom, “but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.” The scattered abroad are the strangers of 1 Peter 1. He gathered both kingdoms together as one. So Caiaphas, who hated the Messiah, prophesied the same thing Christ said: other sheep I have, not of this fold.

Remember Sychar, and Shechem where Abraham built the altar. “There be two manner of nations which my heart abhorreth, and the third is no nation”: the third is no nation at all.

“They that sit upon the mountain of Samaria”: in this context the Greeks, who ruled over Samaria then. “And they that dwell among the Philistines”: the Philistines are Hamites, and he hates them too. “And that foolish people that dwell in Sichem.” That foolish people in Shechem, called no nation: that is the northern kingdom. He calls them not a nation, not a people, and foolish, the very words of Deuteronomy 32: I will move them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will provoke them to anger with a foolish nation.

sense.text: “When thou art come unto the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee, and shalt possess it, and shalt dwell therein, and shalt say, I will set a king over me, like as all the nations that are about me”. This is law: if, when you get into your land, you decide you want a king like all the nations around you, fine.

“Thou shalt in any wise set him king over thee, whom the Lord thy God shall choose”: God has to choose him; you can’t choose him. “One from among thy brethren”: he must be of your people. “Thou mayest not set a stranger over thee, which is not thy brother”: don’t set a heathen over you. That scratches our voting right there.

precepts.why:
Samuel made his sons judges, “And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment.” So “all the elders of Israel gathered themselves together” and said, “now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.”

That is what the law said, so it should not be a problem. Samuel was righteous and a priest. Yet “the thing displeased Samuel”, and he prayed to the Lord. Why would it upset such a righteous man that the people desired something found in the law?

“For they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.” That is why the law is there. The Lord knew Israel would want to be like the other nations, the Hamites, the Arabs, and would reject him and seek a king rather than have him rule over them. But he had something for them: he would come through David’s loins and be king over them anyway, either from the throne up there or the throne down here. The Lord saw it before it happened. And just as Caiaphas said, it was expedient that he should die for that nation.

sense.text:
“But the word of the Lord was unto them precept upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little”. Back then there was no Bible with a table of contents and chapter and verse. There was a scroll for each book: big scrolls, written on animal skin or paper, copied over and over by scribes as they faded. David wrote a hundred and forty-some songs, and that scroll was thick. You read Psalms here and Proverbs there: this goes with this. Daniel read Jeremiah from the scroll and understood the seventy years. That is how they put precepts together; all the prophets were told the same thing, and you put the puzzle together.

“That they might go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken”: broken by that stone of stumbling, that rock of offence; snared and taken by what they are reading, lost in the scriptures.

“Ye scornful men, that rule this people which is in Jerusalem.” This prophecy is towards them that ruled us. The elders would be snared, trapped and fall, because they hated God and hated their people. They were in darkness, and the words of the prophets were darkened to them.

“We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement”: they aligned themselves with the other nations, with the heathen. “For we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves”.
“Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation”. That stone is Christ, the stone Peter spoke of.

“The hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies”: the elders, the rulers. “And your covenant with death shall be disannulled”. Back then it was the Pharisees, the scribes and the elders in bed with Rome; today it is the Christian pastors and the black politicians in bed with America. “Then ye shall be trodden down by it”: overthrown, by Babylon eventually.

“It shall be a vexation only to understand the report.” The report is that Christ is the Messiah, the head of the corner. They were not trying to hear that, because they were in blindness and darkness.

precepts.why:
This is Christ speaking through David about himself on the cross: “They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

“Let their table become a snare before them”: let the rulers’ table be a snare. That is why Isaiah said they would be snared, taken and broken. “Let their eyes be darkened, that they see not”: let the elders’ eyes be darkened, whereunto they were appointed, so that they do not see the Messiah in front of them. When he walked the earth they said, that’s not the guy, it can’t be him.

“Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel”: both the southern and northern kingdoms. “For a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem”: a trap.

“And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken”: the rulers in Jerusalem, who rejected the Messiah because they were evil, sinful and rebellious. That is what Peter quoted: a stone of stumbling. The elders, the builders, the rulers.

“Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?” The heathen, and our people. “The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord, and against his anointed”: the wicked elders and the heathen working together against the Lord, his Son and his disciples.

That is the covenant with death and hell: the rulers in alliance with the heathen oppressors, including trying to save them.

“They are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink. For the Lord hath poured out upon you the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes”. That deep sleep goes back to the darkness, the blindness: closed eyes, you can’t see.

“The prophets and your rulers, the seers hath he covered.” Today that is your priests and pastors, your politicians, your modern-day educators, conservatives and liberals.

“I will praise thee: for thou hast heard me, and art become my salvation.” “art become my salvation” is the stone of verse 22: “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.”

The same stone as Isaiah 28 and Isaiah 8, the rock that begat us in Deuteronomy 32. Not all Israel refused the Lord, and not all the Jews, as the Christians say: the builders refused him, the rulers. He becomes our king and ruler in the end.

“This is the Lord’s doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.” The Lord’s doing is the builders rejecting him, so they would have him killed, to bring in the northern kingdom, to which they were appointed. Write stone here next to Isaiah 28 and tie them together in your notes.

“Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded.” Peter is quoting Isaiah 28:16.

“Unto you therefore which believe he is precious”: the strangers scattered abroad, the elect. “But unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed”: that is Psalms 118. “And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence”: that is Isaiah 8:13-14. Peter is quoting Isaiah and David.

“Even to them which stumble at the word”: the rulers, the builders. The Word is Christ, the same as the Rock. “Whereunto also they were appointed”: predestined to desire a king over them and to reject him. They accepted Rome over Christ, and he died for them anyway.

“Thus saith the Lord concerning the prophets that make my people err”: they teach the wrong thing and prepare war against us. “Therefore night shall be unto you, that ye shall not have a vision”. Night goes back to darkness, your eyes closed, and if you can’t see you stumble and fall. God stops talking to you entirely.

“It shall be dark unto you, that ye shall not divine”: you cannot teach correctly. Now you go to theology school and run to the white man for help. “And the sun shall go down over the prophets, and the day shall be dark over them”: the sun going down means darkness, no understanding. They lose understanding.

Elijah says, “the children of Israel have forsaken thy covenant, thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword; and I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

This shows what the covenant with death and hell means: they were killing the prophets. The rulers taught falsehoods, the prophets came and taught against them, and they killed the prophets.

“But they mocked the messengers of God”: that is what they do now; look at the purple Power Rangers, it is the same thing. “And despised his words”: his law, like they do now. “And misused his prophets”: locked them up, exiled them or killed them in terrible ways. “Until the wrath of the Lord arose against his people, till there was no remedy.”

sense.text: “There dwelt a man in Babylon, called Joacim”.

“Now Joacim was a great rich man, and had a fair garden joining unto his house: and to him resorted the Jews; because he was more honourable than all others.” He was an elder, a leader, and they came to his house to sit with him.

“The same year were appointed two of the ancients of the people to be judges, such as the Lord spake of, that wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges, who seemed to govern the people.” We had ancient judges who came out of Babylon and brought Babylonian doctrine and ideals with them. They seemed to govern the people, but they did not: they were evil and wicked as hell.

These same elders came out of Babylon and made their way into the Roman captivity, and started the Talmud: the Babylonian Talmud. When Christ blasted them for their traditions, they got those from Babylon. These are their fathers here.

precepts.why:
This is where the Lord spoke of it, through Jeremiah: “Hear ye therefore the word of the Lord, all ye of the captivity, whom I have sent from Jerusalem to Babylon”, concerning “Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name”. The king of Babylon would slay them, and the curse would be, “The Lord make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire”. They cooked them to death.

“Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them”. That is what your pastors are doing. The Pharisees did the exact same thing when the Romans ruled: ancient evil out of Babylon, from the elders.

sense.text: “I sent unto you my servants the prophets, whom ye have taken and slain, and torn their bodies in pieces, whose blood I will require of your hands, saith the Lord.” Look what we did to each other: we were killing the prophets of our own people.
“Your house is desolate, I will cast you out as the wind doth stubble. And your children shall not be fruitful; for they have despised my commandment”.

“Your houses will I give to a people that shall come; which not having heard of me yet shall believe me; to whom I have shewed no signs, yet they shall do that I have commanded them.” That is us today. We are born again.

precepts.why: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets”, over and over again, “and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together”: gathered both kingdoms together, “even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!” They refused him: the stone which the builders refused. “Behold, your house is left unto you desolate.”

Stephen prophesies against the rulers, the builders of his time: “as your fathers did, so do ye. Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? and they have slain them which shewed before of the coming of the Just One”. The prophets who prophesied of the Messiah were killed; the killers got away with it and had children, and those children knew who their fathers killed. “Of whom ye have been now the betrayers and murderers”: their fathers killed the prophets who foretold Christ, and when Christ came, they killed him.

“When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth.” Why? Because they knew. Your father killed Zechariah, your father killed Isaiah. They knew and did not care. Stephen was in the spirit and saw it, “being full of the Holy Ghost”, and they were pissed off: who told this man we killed them?

The prophets were supposed to bring us back to God, and the rulers got upset because the prophets could see right through them. It was the same spirit back then.

“But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not take hold of your fathers?” They got so angry at the prophets because the prophets could see right through them, just as in Rome they got mad at the apostles, and at Christ, because they saw right through them. The prophets are the light of the Lord on this earth, and their job is to bring us back to the Father and to his Son Jesus the Christ.

sense.text: A householder planted a vineyard, let it out to husbandmen, and sent his servants to receive the fruits. “And the husbandmen took his servants, and beat one, and killed another, and stoned another.” The servants are the prophets. “Again, he sent other servants more than the first: and they did unto them likewise.”

“But last of all he sent unto them his son, saying, They will reverence my son.” Surely they will respect him above all else. “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance.” If the son is dead, they inherit his inheritance and no one rules over them. “And they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him.”
“He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen”. He is going to get rid of them and hire new people. The other husbandmen are us today.

“Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner”? Now he tells them who the parable is about: I’m talking about you. Have you not read in Psalms what David said about the builders?

“The kingdom of God shall be taken from you”, you elders, “and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof”: the ones Ezra spoke of. “Whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken”: whoever kills him will be broken. “But on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder”: when he returns.
“They perceived that he spake of them.” But “they feared the multitude, because they took him for a prophet.” They couldn’t get him then, but he cut them real bad.

precepts.why: “Your houses will I give to a people that shall come; which not having heard of me yet shall believe me; to whom I have shewed no signs, yet they shall do that I have commanded them.” That is us today: the other husbandmen that render him the fruits.

The same parable again: “So they cast him out of the vineyard, and killed him”: that is Christ. “He shall come and destroy these husbandmen, and shall give the vineyard to others. And when they heard it, they said, God forbid.”

Disrespectful. God forbid we lose our place: we will kill Christ and continue to be the elders and rulers, the heirs. That is how evil the Pharisees were.

sense.text: “Many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.”

“But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness”. The children of the kingdom are the builders, the wicked elders. Outer darkness: closed eyes, the sun going down upon them, as written in Psalms and Isaiah. “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth”: they are going to die terrible deaths, and they are back again today.

precepts.why: This is where it says they shall come from the east and west: “I will bring thy seed from the east, and gather thee from the west; I will say to the north, Give up; and to the south, Keep not back: bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth”. That is to us, Israel.

sense.text:
“Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities.” If it says they are not afraid, it means you should be afraid. There are consequences when you speak evil of Christ, Peter, John the Baptist, James, Paul, Mark, Luke, Stephen, or anyone in the scriptures deemed a prophet or apostle. When you badmouth them, the Lord puts the spirit of darkness on you, and you become a borderline, if not a full-blown, Christianity teacher.

Christ told the apostles they would prophesy again, so be careful how you deal with brothers: you don’t know who you are dealing with. The Lord puts a stumbling block before you for speaking evil of dignities. Brothers bug out and go back into the world for murmuring and speaking evil.

“Having eyes full of adultery, and that cannot cease from sin”: coming in looking for a third, fourth, fifth wife, looking for a mommy to take care of them. “Beguiling unstable souls”: causing confusion. “An heart they have exercised with covetous practices”: money. “Cursed children”.

That is why leaders of other camps who teach a different doctrine do not just show up at our schools unannounced. There are channels. A mature leader would call first and be respectful. A man who shows up uninvited and then throws a tantrum on video for views has shown his true colors. Some of these doctrines can lead you to damnation. We found a GMS member living a double life in one of our schools for months. That is why you cannot be nice all the time.

“These are wells without water”: no understanding. “Clouds that are carried with a tempest”: friends with this one, then over there with that one. “To whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever.” The same darkness that comes when you hate your brother is reserved for them too. That is why people are confused about Cornelius, confused about Romans 11, wound up and confounded in all these basic verses. Keep God’s commandments and laws.

“Three shepherds also I cut off in one month”: the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the scribes, the rulers. The Romans killed them. “And my soul lothed them”: I hated them. “And their soul also abhorred me”: they hated me. It goes back to the builders, the rulers.
“Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not.”

“Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes”: darkness. “lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert”, that is repent, “and be healed.”

precepts.why: “Let them alone: they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.” Leave them alone. Snared and trapped.

“Woe unto you, ye blind guides”. Keep that in mind: blinded, blind, eyes darkened, eyes shut. They say whoever swears “by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor”: they worry about money. “Ye fools and blind”. Christ curses them out the whole chapter.

That is why you’ve got Pastor Pam wearing all black. He is darkened too: dark clothes, a dark spirit, and black eyes under him like a raccoon.

“Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning”. “He that is of God heareth God’s words: ye therefore hear them not, because ye are not of God.” You elders of Satan.

“Say we not well that thou art a Samaritan, and hast a devil?” They called Christ a Samaritan because they hated the northern kingdom. Samaritan was a derogatory term. They called him a devil while they were planning to kill him. That is how evil and conniving they were.

“Not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished”. Moses spent time with the Lord, and the glory of Christ was on him, too blinding to look at. The shine of Moses represented the new covenant: they could not look at Moses the same way they could not see Christ in the Old Testament.

“But their minds were blinded”: not their eyes, their minds. You read the Bible and say, I don’t see it, when it is right there. Nations can’t be saved: I don’t see it. Israelite: I don’t see it. Your mind is blinded. “Until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ.” They are still in the old covenant, blinded when it comes to Christ, and “when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart”: they don’t understand the prophets.

“Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away”: when they repent, they will see Christ. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty”: liberty from keeping animal sacrifice. “We all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord”, the Bible, “are changed into the same image from glory to glory”: a new body in the kingdom.

sense.text: Romans 11 continues from the bottom of chapter 10, which gives its context. “Did not Israel know? First Moses saith, I will provoke you to jealousy by them that are no people, and by a foolish nation I will anger you.” That is Deuteronomy 32. The context is what Israel knows. The you is the southern kingdom; the no people and the foolish nation are the northern kingdom. He would provoke them to anger among themselves. The Lord can be petty sometimes: he is getting at Judah with the northern kingdom, giving them the same blessing. The Lord is a mastermind.
“I was found of them that sought me not; I was made manifest unto them that asked not after me.” That is the northern kingdom, which went into idolatry, and goes back to the provocation of verse 19.

“But to Israel he saith”: the first part was not a people; this is Israel, the southern kingdom. “All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people”: the builders, who would reject Christ.

“I say then”: based on Romans 10:19-21. The northern kingdom sought him not and went into idolatry, and the southern kingdom was disobedient and rejected Christ. So, “Hath God cast away his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.” Paul accepted Christ; God would not have called him into the ministry if he had cast us away. He stresses the tribe of Benjamin because that is the southern kingdom.

“God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew.” Elias cried, “Lord, they have killed thy prophets, and digged down thine altars; and I am left alone”: the same as 1 Kings 19:10, where the killing of the prophets was read earlier. God answered, “I have reserved to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to the image of Baal.” Not all were killed off; some still worshipped him.

“Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.” There will be a remnant of God’s people who serve the Lord against the odds of the wickedness growing on this earth, who will not bow the knee to Baal or accept the mark of the beast. When persecution arises, many Israelites will go back into the world. Right now it is street teaching and making white folks feel bad. But when Trump or his administration turns the heat up, and the Bible or teaching in the streets is outlawed, we will see what everybody is made of and who will not bow to Baal.

“And if by grace, then is it no more of works”. The remnant is called by grace: mercy in Christ. His death and sacrifice granted us grace. The works are the sacrifices and temple ordinances, still going on when Paul wrote, because the temple had not yet been destroyed. We are not called by the animals we sacrifice; we are called by our acceptance of Christ’s death on the cross and of him being the Messiah.

“Otherwise grace is no more grace”: if we still accept the sacrificing of animals, Christ’s death is void; we put Christ to the back. “But if it be of works, then is it no more grace: otherwise work is no more work”: sacrifice is done away with because Christ died on the cross.

“Israel hath not obtained that which he seeketh for; but the election hath obtained it”: the election of grace, those that accept Christ. “And the rest were blinded”: the leaders, who relied on animal sacrifice and temple ceremonies, which they presided over and lived off of from the people. They rejected Christ. “God hath given them the spirit of slumber, eyes that they should not see”: that is to the rulers, the blind Christ spoke of: fools and blind, the blind leading the blind.

Paul quotes more precepts about the elders being blinded: “And David saith, Let their table be made a snare, and a trap, and a stumblingblock”, “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see”. That is Psalm 69:22-23, read earlier.

“Have they stumbled that they should fall?” The they are the leaders, the rulers, with their eyes darkened, stumbling at that stumbling block. Should they fall forever, be cast away? The thought cannot change from verse 1. “God forbid”: their fall is not forever, it is temporary.

“But rather through their fall”, their stumbling at Christ, refusing him and killing him, “salvation is come unto the Gentiles”: the northern kingdom, “for to provoke them to jealousy”: the southern kingdom, the elders. That is what Moses said: I will provoke you to jealousy with them that are not a people. Moses saw this already. It is meant to bring them back together again.

“Now if the fall of them be the riches of the world”: the fall of the builders, the southern kingdom. The world is Israel. The riches of the world are not money; they are the kingdom. The builders had to reject Christ because it was their lot; once Christ died on the cross he granted us access to the kingdom. “And the diminishing of them”: diminishing goes back to the fall, a dropping lower, decay or loss, as the margin of the Cambridge Bible gives it. “How much more their fulness?”: when they all come back together.

“I speak to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office”. Paul’s office was magnified because he taught both Judah and Ephraim. Peter dealt mostly with Judah; Paul and Barnabas went and taught Ephraim, so Paul wrote to the Jews about Christ and to Ephraim about Christ. Paul was also well-versed in different languages.

“If by any means I may provoke to emulation them which are my flesh”. Emulation goes back to jealousy. His flesh is the southern kingdom. By teaching the northern kingdom, he provokes his own flesh to jealousy, “and might save some of them”: the southern kingdom, the leaders. Write verse 11 next to verse 14 and verse 14 next to verse 11, and underline emulation and jealousy, so you know why when you read it.

Paul was raised a Pharisee. The southern kingdom consisted primarily of Levi, Benjamin and Judah, also the leaders, the builders. The top elders were Caiaphas and Annas, and below them their disciples, Gamaliel and Paul.

“For if the casting away of them”: For means because. The casting away goes back to verse 1. “Be the reconciling of the world”. That word should help you very much. Reconcile means to bring back together again what was once together before. So the world here cannot be all nations, because they were never together with us, ever. The world is all Israel, the gathering together of all twelve. Ask them what reconciling means here, and don’t ever leave that verse.

“What shall the receiving of them be, but life from the dead?”: they were dead in their sin, and now they repent of rejecting Christ and come back into the fold.

“For if the firstfruit be holy”: the firstfruit is Christ, our creator, the Rock that begat us; then Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as well. “The lump is also holy”: the lump is Israel. “And if the root be holy”: the root is Christ. “So are the branches”: the branches are us, the offspring, the children.

“And if some of the branches be broken off”: the southern kingdom, because they stumbled and fell. “And thou, being a wild olive tree”: the northern kingdom. That is why Paul magnified his office as the apostle of the Gentiles: he is writing to the southern kingdom but also addressing the northern kingdom in the same letter. “Wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree”: grafting in is reconciling, bringing them back together again. The root and fatness of the olive tree is Christ; both partake of Christ ruling over them.

In literal grafting they cut a space in the tree and set the branch into it, tie it together, and it grows as part of the tree. That is Ezekiel 37:22 and Hosea 1:10. And you can only graft a wild olive tree into an olive tree; you cannot graft a mango tree into an olive tree. The branches are the same. Don’t mingle the seed.

“Boast not against the branches”: Paul is talking to the northern kingdom, who accepted Christ, not to boast against the southern kingdom. “But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee”: if you boast against your brothers, you don’t follow Christ; Christ bears you. “Thou wilt say then, The branches were broken off, that I might be graffed in”: Judah fell off so I could come in, so what? We can replace them. Paul says don’t do that: those are your brothers. That is why the class started with love thy neighbour as thyself. They called Christ a Samaritan as a derogatory term; the hatred was around.

“Because of unbelief they were broken off”: the southern kingdom stumbled. “And thou standest by faith”: you accept Christ, while they held to animal sacrifice. “Be not highminded”, don’t be arrogant, “but fear: For if God spared not the natural branches”: Judah, closer to the Lord through the temple and the priests. “Take heed lest he also spare not thee”: he will cast you off too.

“Behold therefore the goodness and severity of God”. The goodness is Christ dying for them; the severity is them stumbling, falling, shrouded in spiritual darkness, their minds blinded. “On them which fell, severity”: the southern kingdom. “But toward thee, goodness”: the northern kingdom, grafted back in, reconciled through Christ’s death. “If thou continue in his goodness”, that root, Christ: “otherwise thou also shalt be cut off”, as they were cast off in their disobedience.
“And they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be graffed in: for God is able to graff them in again.” Again: they were always there. Grafted in again goes back to reconcile.

“For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature”: the northern kingdom, “and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree”: contrary to nature because they were uncircumcised, in uncleanness, scattered abroad far off. “How much more shall these, which be the natural branches”: the southern kingdom, “be graffed into their own olive tree?” Judah was closer to the Lord, so when they fall off they can come right back. The northern kingdom went into idolatry and is hated by the southern kingdom, so it is harder for them to come back in: they were wild, not a people, Gentile, uncircumcised, heathen.

“That ye should be ignorant of this mystery”. This is why it is so difficult: it is a mystery Moses brought to our attention all the way back in Deuteronomy 32, I will provoke you to jealousy with them which are not a people. “Lest ye should be wise in your own conceits”: highminded, thinking you know everything. “That blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.”

“And so all Israel shall be saved”. That is the conclusion from verse 1 all the way down: he has not cast away his people which he foreknew. The branches grafted in are Israel, and the natural branches are Israel.

“There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob”: all twelve tribes that came from Jacob, not just Judah, Levi and Benjamin. “For this is my covenant unto them, when I shall take away their sins.” Their sins: Jacob’s. The white man did many sins on this earth. Is the Lord going to take away his sins? No. He is going to pay for his sins; judgment is coming on him. Bad news for the nations trying to hide behind Romans 11: none of the nations will make it. The nation of Israel is going to rule over you.

“As concerning the gospel, they are enemies for your sakes”: the southern kingdom were enemies of Christ, for the sakes of the northern kingdom, because they had to reject Christ to bring them back in. “But as touching the election, they are beloved for the fathers’ sakes”: they are still beloved of God, because they are still Israelites.

“For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance. For as ye in times past have not believed God”: that sounds like 1 Peter 2, which in time past were not a people. “Yet have now obtained mercy through their unbelief”: the unbelief of the southern kingdom. “Even so have these also now not believed, that through your mercy they also may obtain mercy. For God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all”: all Israel, as verse 26 says.

precepts.why:
These are the works: “For the shewbread, and for the continual meat offering, and for the continual burnt offering, of the sabbaths, of the new moons, for the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings to make an atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.”

The works Paul speaks of are the sacrifices and temple ordinances. If it is of grace, it is no more of works, because Christ’s death granted us grace.

“The Lord also shall save the tents of Judah first, that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves against Judah.” He raises the tents of Judah first.
“For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first”, Judah first, “and also to the Greek”: the northern kingdom.
“Tribulation and anguish, upon every soul of man that doeth evil, of the Jew first”, Judah first, “and also of the Gentile”: the northern kingdom.

“But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with envy”: jealousy. That is the provoking to jealousy. They “spake against those things which were spoken by Paul, contradicting and blaspheming.”

“It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you”: to the southern kingdom first. “But seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles”: to them which are not a people, the northern kingdom.

You won’t find in the Bible, lo, we turn to the East Indians, or to the Chinese, telling them Christ is black, you’ll be in slavery, the twelve gates don’t have your name, but serve him anyway. Whether you are a black Hebrew Israelite or a Christian, if you teach that, you hate your people. It is not a misunderstanding of the scriptures. He sheweth his word unto Jacob and has not dealt so with any nation, and you still try to find a way to save the people who destroyed, raped, robbed and murdered your people. Muhammad Ali said it about the ten thousand snakes: if a thousand mean no harm but they all look alike, you shut the door.

Some say the world is the world. No, the world is us. “But Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end.” Israel is the world without end.

“But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life.” The world to come is our kingdom, eternal life. Those are the riches of the world.

Life from the dead, because they were dead in their sin: “And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins”. He that quickened is Christ: quickened means brought back to life. That is when they received Christ.
“But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming”: the elect. So the firstfruit of Romans 11 is Christ.
“I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.” Christ is the vine, the root.
“I am the vine, ye are the branches”. The root is Christ, and the branches are us, the offspring, the children: if the root be holy, so are the branches.
Who is the root? “I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David”. Christ is the root.

“Israel is swallowed up: now shall they be among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure.” Then: “For they are gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by himself”. Ephraim is a wild ass alone by himself: a wild ass, a wild olive tree. The northern kingdom is the wild one.

“The Lord called thy name, A green olive tree, fair, and of goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he hath kindled fire upon it, and the branches of it are broken.” The branches broken, just as Paul says.

“For the evil of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah”: the first house and the second house, both houses. So the olive tree is both the house of Israel and the house of Judah. The wild olive tree is not the other nations: they are never called olive trees.

sense.text: This shows Romans 11 easier. Paul writes to the saints which are at Ephesus, and the saints are Israelites. So who is the you? “And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins”: the saints at Ephesus.
“Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air”: the devil.

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” God before ordained that we should walk in the commandments, and he is writing to the Israelites, the saints.

“Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh”. The saints, the Israelites, were in time past Gentiles. In the flesh they were literally uncut: not circumcised, raised in pagan customs, following the course of the world, behaving as the heathen in idolatry. “Who are called Uncircumcision”: not a people, Gentiles. “By that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands”: the southern kingdom, literally cut by hands.

“That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens”: Gentiles, a wild olive tree. Another word for alien is stranger, foreigner, the way they call migrants illegal aliens today. The ten tribes became aliens to the covenant: no longer part of it, because they were far off, foreign, cast off. “From the commonwealth of Israel”: the nation of Israel, which they could no longer take part in; they were not a people any more. “And strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world”: the Lord said to the northern kingdom, ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.

“But now in Christ Jesus”, now that Christ has died, “ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” You are brought near, grafted back in to your brothers, the natural branches.

“For he is our peace”: Christ is the peace between the southern and northern kingdom, against the hatred. “Who hath made both one”: another word for that is reconciliation. “And hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us”: between the northern and southern kingdom.

“Having abolished in his flesh the enmity”: enmity means hatred, the hatred between the southern and northern kingdom. “Even the law of commandments contained in ordinances”: sacrifices, temple law. Under the old covenant the northern kingdom could not be saved: they were condemned, in idolatry, uncircumcised, finished. Christ died on the cross and granted them redemption; otherwise the whole nation would have perished. “For to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace”: twain means two, and the one new man is Israel, all twelve reconciled.
“That he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby”: both kingdoms.

“And came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh”: Christ taught the woman at the well, and he taught the Jews. “For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father”: all Israel, all twelve tribes saved, as in Romans 11.

“Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners”. Not once a heathen, always a heathen: because Christ died, they are no more strangers. “But fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God”: Israelites again, with their brothers. When Christ came and died and Judah rejected him, the northern kingdom got back their citizenship in the kingdom of heaven: naturalized citizens, no longer aliens or strangers. Esau is the illegal alien of this earth.

“And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone”. The foundation is Christ, and the foundation is that all twelve tribes will come together again and be reconciled under one king, under the apostles and prophets that Israelites stumble upon to this day. Christ being the chief corner stone is Christ being our king.

This is why there should be no Christian church. Christ died only for the Israelites, not for Methodists, Baptists, Catholics, Jehovah’s Witnesses, Seventh-day Adventists, Protestants or Lutherans; that is all lies to make you pay tithes. The whole New Testament, and Christ coming and dying, was to bring all twelve tribes together, no other nation. The Gentiles are proved to be Israelites and the world is proved to be the world of Israel. God blinded them and hid it from them, and wanted specific men to bring it out.

precepts.why: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus”. Who is Paul writing to? The saints, and the saints are Israelites. “Grace be to you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.” Now we know who Paul is writing to, with no confusion, and every ye and you in chapter 2 is them.
“Now for a long season Israel hath been without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law.” That sounds like Ephesians: without God, having no hope in the world.

Let’s see who this is: “And he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers with them out of Ephraim and Manasseh, and out of Simeon”. The strangers are out of Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon: the northern kingdom. The strangers of Ephesians 2 are the northern kingdom.

This ties straight into Ephesians 2. “For my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed”: that is Christ, and that is the context.

“Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the Lord, speak, saying, The Lord hath utterly separated me from his people”. That is the northern kingdom: the same as the strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. “Neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I am a dry tree”: they can’t bring forth children.

“Also the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the Lord, to serve him, and to love the name of the Lord, to be his servants, every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant; Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer”. They try to say the heathen will go in there. No: “The Lord God which gathereth the outcasts of Israel saith, Yet will I gather others to him, beside those that are gathered unto him.” Those gathered unto him are this fold; the others are the other sheep not of this fold that Christ spoke of. That is the “all people” of verse 7.

“Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.” The ones afar off.

“O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee, but unto us confusion of faces, as at this day; to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and unto all Israel, that are near, and that are far off”. All Israel: Judah that are near, and the northern kingdom that are far off. So who was near and who was far off? You’ve got it.
